opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it as a kind of complementary axis to what language models have gotten really good at. Language is this incredibly powerful abstraction that humans invented: it's compressed, it's symbolic, and it's a great medium for reasoning about relationships, plans, and ideas. LLMs have shown that if you train on enough of it, you get remarkable abstract reasoning capabilities.

But language is fundamentally a lossy, one-dimensional channel. It's a sequence of tokens. The world we actually live in is three-dimensional, it unfolds over time, and it obeys physics. A lot of what makes humans and animals intelligent happens before language enters the picture. If you watch a kid stack blocks, or think about how you reach for a cup of coffee without spilling it, you're doing an enormous amount of spatial reasoning: understanding geometry, occlusion, depth, how objects move and interact. Very little of that is ever written down, because it's so obvious to us that we never need to describe it.

So when I say spatial intelligence, I mean the ability to perceive, reason about, generate, and interact with the 3D world. It's not that it's opposed to the abstract reasoning in LLMs. I see them as two different pillars. Evolutionarily, spatial intelligence came first. Animals were navigating and manipulating the world for hundreds of millions of years before anything like language existed. Language sits on top of that foundation.

I think there's sometimes an assumption that if you scale language models far enough, spatial understanding just falls out. You do get some of it, since you can ask an LLM about the layout of a room and it'll say something reasonable. But it's operating on descriptions of the world rather than the world itself. If you want models that can build 3D environments, understand a scene from images or video, help robots act, or support designers and architects, you need representations that are natively 3D and natively grounded in how the physical world works.

Long term, the really capable systems will combine both. They'll have the abstract, symbolic reasoning that language gives you and a rich internal model of 3D space and physics. But right now I think spatial intelligence is underexplored relative to language, and that's a big part of why I find it so exciting to work on.

r001.rationale: Defines spatial intelligence as perceiving, reasoning about, generating, and interacting with the 3D world.

r002.rationale: Calls language a lossy, one-dimensional channel and contrasts descriptions of the world with the world itself.

r003.rationale: Says spatial intelligence evolved before language and that much of it seems obvious, but does not attribute people taking it for granted to that evolutionary history.

r004.rationale: Explicitly says language sits on top of the foundation of spatial intelligence.

r005.rationale: Explains that language models reason from descriptions rather than direct experience of the world, leaving a need for grounded spatial understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that language models have gotten really, really good at a particular kind of reasoning, which is reasoning over abstract symbolic concepts. And that's incredible, and it's gotten further than I think most of us expected even a few years ago. But if you look at how intelligence actually developed, both in evolution and in individual humans, language is a very late addition. Animals were navigating the world, understanding how objects move, predicting what happens when you push something off a table, for hundreds of millions of years before anything resembling language showed up. And a toddler has a pretty sophisticated model of the physical world well before they can string a sentence together.

So spatial intelligence, to me, is that whole substrate. It's the ability to perceive the 3D world, to understand its structure, to reason about how it changes over time, to predict the consequences of actions in it, and to actually act in it. And a lot of that is genuinely hard to put into words. If I ask you to describe exactly where every object is in the room you're sitting in, with enough fidelity that someone could reconstruct it, you'd struggle, and you'd produce an enormous amount of text to do a mediocre job. But you can look at the room and know instantly where you can walk and what you can pick up. So the information just lives in a different modality, and it's not clear that the right path to it is routing everything through tokens of text.

That said, I don't think these are in opposition. I think of language as a lossy compression of a richer underlying world model that humans have. When we write about the world, we're emitting a projection of something we understand spatially and physically. LLMs have learned a lot from that projection, which is why they have surprising amounts of implicit physical knowledge. But they've learned it secondhand. And I think the next big frontier is building models that have that grounding firsthand, that have a native representation of 3D space and time, and then combining that with the kind of abstract reasoning LLMs are good at. The abstract reasoning gives you the ability to plan and generalize and communicate. The spatial intelligence gives you something real to reason about.

And practically, for a lot of the things people want AI to do, that grounding is the bottleneck. Robotics, obviously. Design and simulation. Even creative work, where you want to generate a scene that's consistent and that you can move through and edit. Those aren't problems where more text helps you much. They're problems where you need a model that actually understands worlds, not just descriptions of worlds. So that's the gap I spend my time thinking about.

r001.rationale: The response defines spatial intelligence as perceiving and reasoning about the 3D world, predicting action consequences, and acting in it.

r002.rationale: It calls language a lossy compression of a richer world model and says verbal descriptions of a room do a mediocre job compared with direct understanding.

r003.rationale: It mentions that spatial abilities preceded language in evolution, but does not say people take those abilities for granted because of that history.

r004.rationale: It presents language as a projection of a richer spatial and physical understanding, and notes that children develop a physical-world model before speaking.

r005.rationale: It says LLMs learn physical knowledge secondhand from language and argues for firsthand spatial grounding, indicating that text-based reasoning can omit embodied experience.

astra-6.text:
I think of spatial intelligence as the ability to understand and reason about the physical world: where things are, how they relate to one another, and what might happen if you move or interact with them. If I reach for a cup, I need to understand its shape, where it is relative to my hand, and how to pick it up without knocking something else over. There’s a lot of intelligence in that seemingly simple action.

Language gives you a powerful way to reason abstractly, but it leaves many of those details implicit. You can describe a room in words, but that description doesn’t necessarily give you enough information to navigate through it. So I see these as complementary capabilities. Abstract reasoning helps you decide what you want to do; spatial intelligence helps connect that reasoning to the world you actually have to act in.

r001.rationale: It describes reasoning about the physical world and how objects relate, with an example of reaching for and handling a cup.

r002.rationale: It says room descriptions in words leave details implicit and may not provide enough information to navigate.

r003.rationale: It does not connect taking spatial intelligence for granted to human evolutionary history.

r004.rationale: It presents abstract reasoning and spatial intelligence as complementary, but does not say language-based abstraction builds on native spatial understanding.

r005.rationale: In context, it contrasts language-based abstract reasoning with spatial intelligence and says language leaves physical details implicit, suggesting the language route lacks embodied spatial information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of spatial intelligence as the ability to understand and reason about the physical world: where things are, how they relate to one another, and what will happen if you move something or take an action. If I pick up a cup, what’s behind it? If I walk around a table, how does my view change? Those are things people do almost without thinking, but they require a pretty rich understanding of the world.

Language models have shown that you can get surprisingly powerful abstract reasoning from learning patterns in text. But describing a physical situation and actually understanding its spatial structure aren’t necessarily the same thing. You can know the words “behind” and “under” without being able to consistently reason about a scene as the viewpoint changes.

I see these capabilities as complementary. Language gives us a way to express goals and reason at a high level. Spatial intelligence connects that reasoning to perception and action. The interesting question is how to bring them together so a system can both talk through a problem and understand what its answer means in the physical world.

r001.rationale: It describes understanding physical objects and spatial relations through actions such as picking up a cup or walking around a table, including how the view changes.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes describing a physical situation from understanding its spatial structure, but does not clearly state that verbal descriptions are a lossy representation of embodied spatial experience.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute people’s tendency to take spatial intelligence for granted to evolutionary history.

r004.rationale: It presents language and spatial intelligence as complementary, but does not say language-based abstraction builds on humans’ native spatial understanding.

r005.rationale: It says text-based language models can reason abstractly while still failing to consistently reason about scenes, and that spatial intelligence connects reasoning to perception and action.
